While Everyone Was Watching Kimi K3 and DeepSeek, Google Quietly Shipped Its Own Open-Weight Model. It’s Already Beating Bigger Competitors. Here’s Why This Matters More Than It Looks.

3 min read
Just now

--

For weeks, the open-versus-closed AI debate has had a clear shape: Chinese labs like Moonshot and DeepSeek shipping free, open-weight models at frontier scale, while Western labs — Google very much included — stayed closed, API-only, subscription-gated. That framing just got a lot less accurate.
Google DeepMind released Gemma 4, a family of four open models — E2B, E4B, a 26B mixture-of-experts model, and a 31B dense model — purpose-built for advanced reasoning and agentic workflows, all licensed under Apache 2.0. Built on the same underlying technology as Gemini 3, the models deliver strong intelligence-per-parameter, with the 31B model ranking #3 globally among open models on the Arena AI text leaderboard, and the 26B model at #6.
Apache 2.0 — one of the most permissive open-source licenses that exists. Not a research preview. Not a limited API. Actual open weights, ranking in the global top ten against every other open model in the world, including the much larger, much-more-discussed releases from Chinese labs this month.

Why This Contradicts the Narrative Almost Everyone Has Been Running With
The story of the last six weeks has been consistent: Kimi K3’s 2.8 trillion parameters stunning the industry, DeepSeek V4 going stable, the entire “tokenmaxxing crackdown” being framed as a shift toward cheap, open Chinese alternatives specifically because Western labs stayed closed and expensive. That framing wasn’t wrong about the trend. It was incomplete about who’s actually participating in it.
Google shipping a genuinely competitive, permissively licensed open model — built on the same technology stack as its flagship closed product — is a meaningfully different move than anything else Google has done this year. It’s not a defensive PR gesture. It’s a real, rankable, benchmarked entry into the exact category that’s been driving the biggest cost and access conversations in AI all summer.

Why the Smaller Model Sizes Are the Actually Interesting Part
Here’s the detail worth paying more attention to than the leaderboard ranking: E2B and E4B are genuinely small. NVIDIA confirmed day-one optimization for RTX GPUs, DGX Spark, and Jetson edge devices — meaning these models are built to run on consumer and edge hardware, not just data-center-scale infrastructure.
That’s a different value proposition than Kimi K3’s 2.8-trillion-parameter scale, which requires serious dedicated hardware to self-host meaningfully. Gemma 4’s smaller variants are aimed at exactly the use case most individual developers and small teams actually have: something capable enough to be genuinely useful, small enough to run on hardware they already own, and free enough that the per-token cost conversation stops mattering entirely.

What This Means for the Comparison You Should Actually Be Running
If your mental model of “open AI models” has been “Chinese labs versus closed Western labs,” Gemma 4 is a good reason to update that model today. The open-weight landscape now includes a genuinely competitive Google entry, sitting in the global top ten, built on frontier technology, licensed as permissively as it gets.
aiexpo.app — 1,600-plus tools, 70-plus categories, over 1,080 completely free, updated every single day — already has this comparison laid out honestly, across every lab, every license, and every model size.

The assumption that open-weight AI is a race happening somewhere else, between Chinese labs and each other, just got harder to defend. Google shipping a top-ten open model, on the same day everyone’s still talking about Kimi K3, is a reminder that the most important shifts in AI this year keep arriving quietly, a few days after the louder headline already set the narrative.
